candidates.title: Curb Verdict
candidates.pitch: A pole of stacked parking plates stands on an invented street, a stone gargoyle perched on top, and the visitor must rule on each case: may this car, with this permit, at this day and hour, stay, and until when? Behind the jokes is a real rules engine that merges time windows, day masks, permits and street-cleaning slots into a week-long legality strip, so every wrong answer shows exactly which plate decided it. A second mode, Sign Smith, hands you a target pattern and a plate budget and scores how few plates reproduce it.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. Rescues a universally groaned-at subject (parking rules) by turning rule-reading into a deduction puzzle with a deadpan gargoyle judge.

research.summary: Search results show confusing stacked parking signs are a recurring complaint in several countries, and that phone apps now read photographed signs, yet no game or quiz about decoding them turned up. Reading guides describe layered plates of days, time windows, permit exceptions, street-cleaning slots and arrows. The page will use an invented municipal code and invented sign vocabulary (no real jurisdiction, no real signage), so the engine is fully specified by the page itself and the real-world sources only establish that the pain and the gap are real.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-10, news reports from the UK (ITV, 2024-12-04) and US cities (Washington DC, Chicago) describe drivers and officials struggling with confusing parking signs.
As of 2026-10-10, search found phone apps that decode photographed parking signs (a Montreal team's app, Parky.AI) but no game or quiz built around decoding them.
Reported by one guide, unconfirmed: stacked plates are read top to bottom, with day plates, time windows and permit wording each changing the answer.
Reported by one catalog entry, unconfirmed: a 2009 New York user study found existing signs mismatched drivers' mental models.

inspirations: gargoyle judge on a cathedral roof

design.coreLoop: Each case shows a pole, a car with a permit type, and a day and time. The visitor chooses stay or leave and then the latest legal departure time on a week strip. The engine reveals the deciding plate and the full legality timeline, and the gargoyle comments. Cases escalate from one plate to six, with generated traps (exception plates, overnight windows that wrap midnight, cleaning slots that bite only on one weekday) so minute ten feels different from minute one. Sign Smith mode inverts it: build a stack to match a target legality pattern with the fewest plates.
sophisticationHooks: Rules engine: each plate is {action, day mask, minute window (may wrap midnight), permit exceptions, limit}; the week is 10080 minutes, rules are compiled into merged intervals, and precedence is the most restrictive active plate, with an explain trace naming the deciding plate
Seeded case generator (mulberry32 from the date or a hash seed) that uses the solver to guarantee a unique answer and a difficulty score based on how often the naive top-plate reading is wrong
Sign Smith inverse mode: a small search (greedy plus bounded brute force over plate templates) computes the minimum plate count, so the visitor's score is relative to the optimum
Week legality strip and explain overlay that make the logic visible; shareable URL hash holds seed, mode and answers
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: pure rules module (compile, evaluate, explain, generate, solve), SVG pole and gargoyle art drawn by hand, Verdict mode with about 40 generated cases per seed, Sign Smith mode with 12 target patterns, share link, about/making-of panel, light/dark, reduced motion, keyboard play. Cut: multiple cities, real signage, sound beyond one soft stamp sound, accounts, streak sync.
risks: Must use an invented jurisdiction and invented plate styling; no real sign designs, no legal advice, with a visible note that the in-game code is fictional
Rule-precedence ambiguity could make answers feel unfair; mitigated by printing the in-game municipal code and showing the explain trace
Reported guide specifics and the 2009 study remain unverified, so the page cites them only as 'as of 2026-10-10, per <source>' or omits them

candidates.title: The Waiting Hum
candidates.pitch: A calm little waiting room whose arrivals and departures are played as soft notes: run it at low load and it sounds like a slow lullaby, push the load toward capacity and the tune swells, stutters and collapses into a tangle. The visitor staffs the counters, chooses one shared line or separate lines, and tunes how erratic arrivals and service are, trying to keep the average wait under a target on a budget. A live panel compares the running simulation with the textbook formulas, so the famous knee in the waiting-time curve is something you hear and see.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. Queue theory is the textbook definition of a dud subject, rescued by letting the visitor hear a system approach saturation.

research.summary: Standard university sources agree on the M/M/1 results (mean number in system rho/(1-rho), time 1/(mu-lambda), both diverging as utilization approaches 1) and on Little's law holding regardless of distributions. Kingman's approximation adds a variability term that lets the page show why erratic arrivals or service inflate waits. Operations writing supports the pooled single line for reducing wait variability while noting people prefer it partly for fairness. Parameter-mapping sonification is an established technique with a known caution about quantizing to scales. The sim computes truth; the formulas run alongside as a check.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-10, course materials agree that an M/M/1 queue is stable only when utilization is below 1, with mean number in system rho/(1-rho) and mean time in system 1/(mu-lambda), both growing without bound as utilization nears 1.

As of 2026-10-10, Kingman's approximation puts mean wait in a G/G/1 queue near rho/(1-rho) times the average of arrival and service squared variability times mean service time, and is most accurate near saturation.

As of 2026-10-10, operations sources report that a single pooled line feeding several servers reduces wait variability, though separate lines can feel faster when one's own lane moves and pooling gains are weaker for people who can switch lanes.
Reported, unconfirmed: the Erlang C model gives the wait probability for N servers at offered load A and assumes Poisson arrivals, exponential service and no abandonment.
Reported, unconfirmed: parameter-mapping sonification maps data points to pitch, and quantizing to a scale can distort the data.

design.coreLoop: Set arrival pressure, number of counters, line layout (pooled or separate), and variability, then run a seeded shift. Arrivals and service completions play notes while a canvas shows people queueing; at the end the page scores mean and 90th percentile wait against the target and the budget. Levels hand over constraints (a rush hour profile, a lunch break that removes a counter, a slow-service burst) so the visitor keeps learning why waits explode near full load and what variability and pooling buy.
sophisticationHooks: Discrete-event simulation with a binary-heap event list, seeded mulberry32 RNG, exponential and tunable-variance service and arrival distributions, multi-server with pooled or join-shortest-line policies, run in a worker to stay smooth

Live theory overlay: M/M/1 and approximate Kingman curves and a Little's-law check (average number equals rate times average time) plotted against the running simulation so the visitor sees them converge

Sonification: arrivals and departures map to notes of a consonant scale, wait length to harmonic tension, with scale quantization declared in the making-of panel; a calm mode and a mute default for autoplay policy
Shift-profile challenges with a scoring rule and shareable URL hash (seed, servers, layout, variability)
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: pure sim core with tests-by-reasoning, worker wrapper, canvas queue scene, WebAudio synth with hand-made envelopes, theory overlay with two curves, 8 challenge shifts, share link, light/dark, reduced motion (no flashing, static chart fallback), keyboard controls, about/making-of panel. Cut: abandonment and priority classes beyond one toggle, exact multi-server Kingman, recorded audio, account scores.
risks: Audio must start only after a user gesture and be muted-safe; a visual-only fallback of equal clarity is required

Erlang C specifics and sonification caveats remain unverified, so the page shows them as 'as of 2026-10-10, per <source>' or omits them; the simulation is the source of truth for all displayed numbers
Worker performance with long runs; mitigated by capping event counts and batching the posted frames
